column1: Several terms are not linear in x — peak is a max and aFRR is a curve — so Valuation must publish functions rather than scalars and bounds rather than just prices.

If Valuation published arbitrary delegates the Planner could not embed them in a MILP and would have to sample them, and sampling a function to build a MILP is slow, lossy, and silently changes the problem being solved.
If Valuation publishes scalars, the economics are wrong.
Valuation emits a closed, small algebra of exactly five shapes that a MILP can ingest natively, and nothing else.
Every view's published field table resolves to a set of the five shapes.
A LinearTerm carries a coefficient per (decision variable, slot), is realised as an objective coefficient, and introduces no binaries.

A PwlTerm carries breakpoints, a curvature in {Concave, Convex, General} and a sense in {Max, Min}, is realised by a λ-formulation that is an exact LP if curvature matches sense and SOS2 otherwise, and introduces binaries only if the curvature is General.

An EpigraphTerm carries a variable name, a set of slots it must dominate, a floor value and a unit price, is realised as z ≥ expr[t] for all t together with z ≥ floor and cost c·z, and introduces no binaries.
A BoundTerm carries a lower or upper bound on a decision variable or on a linear expression per slot, is realised as a constraint, and introduces no binaries.
A CouplingConstraint carries a declared structural constraint spanning decision variables, is realised as constraint rows, and introduces binaries only where declared.
Nothing crosses C2 except the five shapes: no delegates, no scenario arrays, no Belief handles and no object.
Every shape is a serialisable value type with a declared schema.
PeakView maps to an EpigraphTerm, because max is linear in epigraph form: z_peak ≥ p_poi[t] for all t in the window, z_peak ≥ realisedPeak, with objective −peakPrice · z_peak.
The peak epigraph formulation needs no binaries and no max operator and is exact.
The peak epigraph floor is precisely peak_to_go, which is why the peak term must be composed last.
AfrrCapacity maps to a concave PwlTerm with sense Max plus a BoundTerm for the MW envelope.
The expected value of the aFRR capacity bid curve V(E) is concave in offered MW under a standard clearing model, so it embeds with no binaries.
AfrrEnergy and ImbalanceRisk map to a LinearTerm per scenario plus a convex PwlTerm with sense Min for the risk functional.
CVaR is representable as a linear program by the Rockafellar–Uryasev formulation, so a CVaR-penalised objective stays a MILP.
IdOption maps to a PwlTerm in volume, concave because the marginal MWh gets a worse price, plus a BoundTerm from SOC and efficiency feasibility.
OppCost maps to a LinearTerm for cycle cost per throughput, a concave Max PwlTerm for V(SOC), and a BoundTerm for power and POI limits.
FillProbView maps to a BoundTerm only: it constrains how much intraday volume may be counted on and carries no price.
The type system enforces that FillProbView carries no price, because a BoundTerm has no price field to populate.
Tariff and stamp map to a LinearTerm set that is closed and enumerated per tick.
Each PwlTerm declares its curvature and the composer verifies it against the breakpoints.
A term declaring Concave with a non-concave breakpoint set is a contract violation, not a silently-wrong relaxation.
Whether a PWL needs binaries — and therefore whether the solve takes 200 ms or 200 s — depends entirely on the declared curvature being true.

The Planner's problem class is known statically: from the shapes present the engine can report before solving the number of binaries, whether the model is an LP, and which term introduced each binary.
Solve-time regressions become attributable to an economic modelling choice rather than mysterious.
Valuation can express genuinely non-linear economics without knowing anything about MILP formulation, and the Planner can ingest them without knowing what an aFRR bid curve is.
Adding a new economic lever means adding a view that emits existing shapes.
A lever that cannot be expressed in the five shapes is a design conversation, not a quiet delegate.
Breakpoint count is a tuning knob with a measurable accuracy/speed trade-off.
Some economics require care to express in the five shapes, and this is the intended friction.
Delegates or callbacks into Valuation are not embeddable in a MILP, not serialisable, not replayable, and let Valuation smuggle Belief state across the seam.
Scalars only give the wrong economics for peak, reserve and option value — the three terms the whole system exists to trade off.
Letting the Planner own the economics collapses two layers into one and makes the too-complicated-to-just-find-the-optimum problem inevitable.
A general expression tree would require the Planner to run a full interpreter and it could no longer guarantee the problem class or bound the binaries.
The closed algebra buys static analysability, which is worth more than generality here.
The composer applies terms in the fixed order tariff, then opp-cost plus λ_SOC, then peak_to_go last, then validate.
Peak headroom must be priced on top of a battery whose energy is already marked with its opportunity cost, and reversing the order would double-count.
An ordering convention is fragile because it is a fact about the code that must be remembered.
An economic effect counted twice produces a plausible number, passes every type check, and biases the strategy in a direction that looks like profit.
Energy is priced by OppCost as internal cost and by the spot views as market value, and if both mark the same MWh arbitrage appears free.
aFRR capacity reserves SOC headroom that IdOption may also plan to use.
The peak term prices POI import that the tariff term also prices per MWh, and these are legitimately two different charges only if each is applied to its own base.
Degradation may be charged by OppCost per throughput and again inside V(SOC) if the value function was fitted on net-of-degradation cashflows.
Every emitted term declares what it prices, and the composer rejects any bundle in which one (effect, decision variable, slot) triple is priced more than once.

Each term carries an EconomicEffect tag from the closed enumeration SpotEnergyValue, IdEnergyValue, ReserveCapacityRevenue, ReserveEnergyRevenue, ImbalanceCost, NetworkPeakCharge, NetworkVolumetricCharge, LeviesAndTaxes, EnfgLevies, SubsidyRevenue, CycleDegradation, StoredEnergyContinuation and ActivationRisk.
Every economic effect maps to exactly one owning view and never to the Planner, which adds no economics of its own.
The term ownership matrix in L2 §5 is a normative table mapping each effect to exactly one owning view.
The composer asserts coverage: every effect in the active configuration is claimed by exactly one view.
An unclaimed effect is a warning, and the tick proceeds with the effect priced at zero and the omission logged, because silently missing revenue is safer than silently double-counting cost.
The composer asserts exclusivity: no effect is claimed twice for the same (variable, slot), and violation is a hard failure rather than a warning.
Terms declare the base they apply to, from PoiImport, BatteryThroughput, MarketVolume, TerminalSoc, ReserveCapacity and Delineation.
A volumetric network charge on PoiImport and a peak charge on PoiImport are both legal because they are different effects on the same base, while two NetworkPeakCharge terms on the same base are not.
LeviesAndTaxes on PoiImport and EnfgLevies on Delineation are legal and are not a double count, because they are disjoint component lists on disjoint bases.
The reducible EnFG components are charged on (21), and what a delineation regime cannot reduce stays on PoiImport.
Relief is never booked as revenue: (20) is a diagnostic quantity, not an effect.
Composition ordering is a declared, verified property rather than a convention, with each stage declaring preconditions and postconditions.
Stage 1, Tariff, requires nothing and establishes that POI energy is fully marked.
Stage 2, OppCost plus V(SOC), requires POI energy marked and establishes that battery energy is marked and terminal value attached.
Stage 3, Reserve coupling, requires battery energy marked and establishes that SOC corridor constraints are present.
Stage 4, Peak epigraph, requires both POI energy marked and battery energy marked, and establishes that the peak variable is bounded below by the realised peak.
Stage 5, Validate, requires all previous stages and establishes that the bundle is well-formed and complete.
If a stage's preconditions are unmet, composition fails loudly, so running the stages in the wrong order produces an exception rather than a wrong number.
The ordering rule is enforced by the machine, so it survives refactoring, new contributors, and agent-authored changes.
Adding a view requires updating the ownership matrix, which forces the question of what it prices and who else prices it at the right moment.
The ownership matrix doubles as the basis for Settlement's P&L attribution, with realised P&L decomposed into the same effect enumeration so planned and realised value are comparable term by term.
Comparability of planned and realised value term by term is what makes the four-bucket error decomposition possible.
The ownership matrix costs a tag on every term and a matrix to maintain.
A documented ordering convention is correct but unenforced.
A single monolithic pricing function has no double-count risk but is untestable and unextendable.
Post-hoc reconciliation only catches double-counting after the fact, in aggregate, long after the bad decisions were taken.
Plugging everything into one solver and asking for the optimum is not doable at operational speed.

aFRR capacity is committed for coarse blocks well before the intraday information that determines the spot opportunity cost arrives, so the capacity decision is a first-stage decision under uncertainty.
Reserve does not consume energy but consumes power headroom and SOC corridor.
Every MW of upward reserve held is a MW that cannot be sold on the spot market and a block of SOC that cannot be traded away, for the whole delivery block.
Committed reserve turns into energy at random, correlated with exactly the prices that make the energy valuable elsewhere.
The joint problem is hard at the scale of scenarios times slots times binaries.
Pre-allocating capacity is a primal restriction that deletes options from the feasible set.
If the pre-allocated capacity is wrong the loss is unbounded and invisible, because the spot MILP reports a clean optimum over a feasible set that was silently amputated.
The correct instrument is a dual price: charge the spot problem for the headroom it consumes, at a price that reflects what aFRR would have paid for it.
Dual pricing weakly dominates primal restriction: it recovers the same solution when the allocation happens to be right and does better whenever it is wrong.
The dual price is the internal transfer price of a MW of battery headroom, and it is where the edge over less careful participants lives.
There are three co-optimisation tiers behind one interface, ICoOptimizer, with a mandatory measured gap between them.
In Tier 1 the reserve capacities per block r_up[b] and r_dn[b] are decision variables alongside spot dispatch in one joint stochastic MILP.
The power headroom coupling constraints are p_d[t] + r_up[b(t)] ≤ P_max_dis and p_c[t] + r_dn[b(t)] ≤ P_max_chg for all t.
The POI envelope constraint is p_poi[t] within [−E_exp, E_imp] for all t.
The SOC corridor constraints are soc[t] − r_up[b(t)]·D/η_d ≥ soc_min and soc[t] + r_dn[b(t)]·D·η_c ≤ soc_max for all t.
On the activation path soc evolves under scenario-s activation and soc[s,t] stays within [soc_min, soc_max] for a weighted fraction of at least (1−ε) of scenarios, as a chance constraint.
The peak constraints in Tier 1 are z_peak ≥ p_poi[t] for all t and z_peak ≥ realisedPeak.
D, the sustained-delivery requirement from prequalification, is a calendar parameter and not a constant.
Tier 1 is the accuracy reference and does not need to be fast, because its job is to be right and to serve as the oracle everything else is scored against.
Tier 1 runs offline on every backtest day regardless of which tier ships.
Tier 2 relaxes the coupling constraints with multipliers μ_up[b] and μ_dn[b], separating the problem into a spot subproblem and a reserve subproblem.
The Tier 2 spot subproblem is a fine-grained MILP over 15-minute slots, charged μ times the headroom consumed for the resource it uses.
The Tier 2 reserve subproblem is a small, near-analytic problem over coarse blocks: offer reserve where expected capacity revenue plus expected activation value exceeds μ.
μ is iterated with a subgradient or bundle method to primal feasibility.
μ* is the reservation price and is provably consistent with spot opportunity cost: it is the marginal value of headroom in the spot problem, not a heuristic weighting.
At any iteration the Lagrangian dual value gives an upper bound on the true optimum, so the gap to the best primal solution is a number that can be reported.
The decomposition matches the natural structure of coarse reserve blocks and fine spot slots, and the subproblems are each far easier than the joint model.

Tier 3 fits μ̂ = f(features) offline on Tier 1 and Tier 2 solutions across a long history, with features being calendar position, price-level and spread beliefs, reserve-price beliefs, SOC, peak headroom and qualification state.
At runtime Tier 3 evaluates μ̂, prices the headroom, and solves one spot MILP.
Tier 3 is the pre-allocate-then-narrow-then-solve idea with the allocation replaced by a price and with a number attached to what it costs.
The reservation-price surface f is a materialised artefact: versioned, content-hashed, and exportable to a form C# evaluates natively.
No tier ships without its gap measured against Tier 1.
The gap distribution over a holdout backtest is reported per release as p50, p90, p99 and worst case, never as a mean, because the tail is where a fast heuristic destroys value.

The gap is reported conditioned on regime — high-spread days, peak-critical days, high reserve price days — because a heuristic that is fine on average and terrible on the ten days that matter is worse than useless.
The distance from Tier 1 to a perfect-foresight upper bound is reported, which separates a weak optimiser from an uncertain world.

Escalation is automatic: ICoOptimizer may escalate at runtime if Tier 3's solution is near a coupling constraint boundary, or the state is out of the training distribution, or the peak-critical flag is set.
An escalated tick escalates to Tier 2 within its time budget.
The system has a defensible answer to how good its approximation is at all times.
The three tiers share one interface, so the production tier is a configuration choice and a backtest can run all three for comparison on the same data.
Tier 2's μ* is diagnostically valuable in its own right as an interpretable internal price a human can sanity-check, unlike a black-box policy.
Tier 1 must exist even though it may never run in production, because without an oracle there is no gap and without a gap there is no engineering.
Subgradient convergence needs a step-size rule, an iteration cap, and a guaranteed feasible primal recovery on every exit path.
Hard pre-allocation by heuristic is primal restriction with invisible, unbounded loss.
Sequential markets in priority order are a special case of hard pre-allocation, with the allocation set by an arbitrary ordering.
End-to-end reinforcement learning has no feasibility guarantee, no certifiable gap, is unreplayable, and is impossible to explain to a risk function.
Reinforcement learning may have a place inside Tier 3's f, where its output is a price checked against an oracle, but not as the decision maker.
Tier 1 only is correct and probably too slow, and until the latency budget is fixed this cannot be claimed otherwise.
The tier ladder makes the latency-budget decision deferrable without blocking design.
